albert-thomas-fairmont-1900-08-11.A1:
A LYNCHING PROBABLE.
Two Railroad Men Shot by Colored Tramps.
FAIRMONT. W. Va., Aug. 11.—Henry Downey, Baltimore and Ohio yardmaster here, and John Lilly, a well-known Baltimore and Ohio detective, were shot this afternoon in the company's yard by two colored tramps, Albert Thorne, who claims to be from New York, and Charles Campbell, of South Dakota. Downey will probably die, being shot through the abdomen and in the arm, but Lilly may recover.

Immediately after the shooting the negroes ran to the woods at the upper end of the yards. Three engines were hastily manned and sent in as many different directions. The fugitives were captured and, when brought to town, were surrounded by an angry mob. The situation is considered critical by the authorities, for large crowds are standing sullenly about the principal thoroughfares awaiting Downey's death.

On Friday night the negroes attempted to shoot Baltimore and Ohio men at Farmington and later at Mannington, because they would not permit them to ride on the trains.

At a late hour tonight Downey's physicians had not located the ball that entered his abdomen. If he dies the negroes will undoubtedly be lynched.
albert-thomas-fairmont-1900-08-11.A2:
Special to the Register. FAIRMONT W. Va.
Special to the Register.

FAIRMONT, W. Va., August 11.

Baltimore & Ohio Detective Charles Lilley, of Grafton, and Henry Downey, a Baltimore & Ohio employee here, were probably fatally shot by two negroes at 4 o'clock this evening.

Last evening at Farmington they, along with three white men, made an attempt to board an east-bound freight, but were prohibited from doing so by the brakeman. They fired several shots at the brakeman, without effect.

They were found here this evening at 4 o'clock, and the detective and Downey made an attempt to arrest them. They succeeded in getting free and when a short distance away they began pouring lead from 32 and 38 calibre revolvers, each and every shot taking effect.

Downey is probably the worst injured of the two. He was shot in the breast and arm, while he was hit in the side and arm. Lilley's cries for help brought to their assistance an immense crowd, but the would-be murderers fled.

A search was instituted by Chief Fleming and the police, Yardmaster Riggs, Constable Jones, and others, and the murderers were captured. The negroes were captured quite a distance above town hd in bushes. They confess to having done all the shooting here to-day. The wounded men are in a serious condition.

The citizens are aroused and if either of the men dies in all probability the negroes will be lynched.
But little hopes are entertained for
their recovery.
albert-thomas-fairmont-1900-08-11.A3:
PRISONERS TAKEN TO COUNTRY.
Downey Will Hardly Survive His Wounds-Other Man Not so Badly Hurt-Great Excitement Prevails. Culprits May Yet Fall at the Hands of the Mob.
Special Dispatch to the Intelligencer.

Special Dispatch to the Intelligencer.
FAIRMONT, W. Va., Aug. 12.—An attempt was made at lynching the two negroes who shot Henry Downey and Charles Lilley at the Baltimore & Ohio freight depot here yesterday while resisting arrest. A large crowd visited the jail with this object in view, but the prisoners had been taken to the country, where they were kept in hiding by the officers until this morning, when they were returned to town and removed elsewhere. After searching the jail and raising considerable disturbance the crowd dispersed. The negroes are not known here, but they gave their names as Albert Thomas, of Philadelphia, and George Campbell, of Colorado. They are both young. Downey, who is it thought will not survive his wounds is about thirty-eight years old and is very popular. He has a wife and child. Lilley is not so badly hurt and will recover.
albert-thomas-fairmont-1900-08-11.A5:
FAIRMONT MOB.
Enters the jail After Two Color- ed Men.
But Fails to Find Them-The Men had Shot Two B. & O. Employees-Great Excitement in Fairmont Over the Crime-Men Were Smuggled out of Town and Taken to Moundsville.
Fairmont was the scene of a shooting scrape at four o'clock on Saturday afternoon and it came near being the scene of a lynching bee that night. The removal of the two shooters was all that prevented a mob from hanging them without waiting the process of law.

B. & O. detective Charles Lilley, of Grafton, is one of the injured men and Henry Downey, one of the railroad employees at Fairmont is the other. Downey is hurt worse than Lilley having been shot in the breast and arm while the other man received shots in the side and arm.

The shooting grew out of the attempt to arrest several tramps. They had tried to board a freight train at Farmington on Friday evening and when put off had fired at the trainmen. They reported the matter and the detective was put on the track.

He traced them to Fairmont and together with Downey attempted to arrest them. They resisted and a general fusilade took place. Both the injured men were too badly hurt to follow. them up but their cries for assistance brought a number of railroad men who took the negroes into camp.

They were lodged in jail and excitement got to fever heat. It was reported during Saturday night that Downey had died and a mob of five hundred men at once started for the jail to hang the murderers.

The officials had feared this move however and they had removed the prisoners to Moundsville where they are at present. The mob searched the jail and not being able to find the men it then dispersed. It was reported that the men had been brought to Morgantown but this was a mistake. At last accounts Downey was still alive and it is thought that he has a better chance for recovery than at first anticipated. The excitement in Fairmont is cooling down a great deal but had the guilty men been obtained by the mob they would have been hung without delay.
albert-thomas-fairmont-1900-08-11.A7:
THREATENED WITH LYNCHING.
TWO COLORED PRISONERS WERE BROUGHT HERE FROM FAIRMONT LAST EVENING.
FIGURED IN THE SHOOTING
Which Resulted in Detective Lilley, of Grafton, and B. & O. Employe Downey Being Seriously Wounded—One of the Negroes Admitted That He Shot to Scare the Two Men—Both Prisoners Interviewed Last Night.
The two negroes, George Campbell and Albert Thomas, who were arrested Saturday evening at Fairmont, charged with shooting B. & O. Detective Charles Lilley, of Grafton, and Henry Downey, a B. & O. employee, are now in the Ohio county jail, having been brought to this city over the B. & O. road last evening about half past six o'clock, in charge of four deputy sheriffs. This action was taken by the authorities because of the fact that the two prisoners were threatened with lynching while in the jail at Fairmont yesterday morning about two o'clock.

According to a special dispatch to the Register from Fairmont, a crowd of four hundred people gathered around the county jail there while the building was being searched for the two negroes. It is learned that it was their intention to lynch them if found, and the county officers quickly realizing the situation, hastily took the two prisoners to a place called Gray's Flats, thence to Barracksville, where tickets were purchased for Moundsville, and finally brought them here.

A Register reporter visited the cells of the two men last night, and both were reluctant to discuss the case in detail. Both men had lain down for a rest, and refused to get up while they were being interviewed.

Campbell seemed inclined to evade direct questions and with considerable hesitancy stated that he and Thomas were arrested for shooting, but did not shoot at any one. When asked if he thought there was any cause for his arrest, he replied that he would not talk about it yet as he had plenty of time. He said that his home was at Larimore, North Dakota, and that his parents are dead.

When questioned Thomas said that he did not know the nature of the charge against him, but admitted that he figured in the shooting. He said that as soon as he saw the detective coming toward him, accompanied by another man, that he drew a revolver, which he carried, and shot to scare them. He also stated that he used a 38 calibre revolver, and thought the detective meant to arrest him for vagrancy. The prisoner said that Philadelphia, Pa., was his home, and he had been on the road since last March, moving from one place to another. He had no occupation, but depended on odd jobs for a livelihood. He had met Campbell about a month ago, and they had been together constantly since then. He also stated that he had never stolen anythings and had always managed to earn enough money to buy something to eat.

Campbell is twenty-two years old and Thomas only seventeen years of age. Both stated that they were badly frightened when the crowd surrounded the jail at Fairmont, and were anxious to get away.

As reported in the telegraphic columns of yesterday's Register Detective Lilley and B. & O. employe Downey were seriously injured, receiving wounds from 32 and 38 calibre revolvers. It was learned late last night that Lilley will recover, but Downey will probably die.

The two negroes, it is said, together with three white men, attempted to board a freight train at Farmington Saturday night, and being prohibited from doing so, fired at the brakeman, without effect. The detective and Downey found the negroes at Fairmont and endeavored to arrest them.
albert-thomas-fairmont-1900-08-11.A10:
LILLY TALKS
About the Tragedy at Fairmont Saturday.
Sorry he Was not able to Hit His Assailants-Downey Recovering-Special Grand Jury to be Called-Memorandum Book Saves Lilly's Life-Shooters Said to be Professionals.
FAIRMONT, W. Va., Aug. 15. — Excitement over the assault upon Henry Downey and Charles Lilly, the Baltimore & Ohio employees, has disappeared. This is due to the fact that Downey continues to improve and every indication is that he will pull through without difficulty. It is feared that one of the bullets punctured the bowels and if such is the case inflammation may prove fatal. The physicians state, however, that careful nursing can prevent such a catastrophe and the B. & O. railroad company has secured the services of a trained nurse for Downey.

Lilly is painfully, but not seriously, hurt. A bullet is still embedded in the bone of his left arm and he will probably have to go to a Baltimore hospital to have it extracted. The wound over his heart is little more than a bruise. Lilly, while still confined to his bed, is able to receive visitors and can talk intelligently of the affair. He said to a reporter:

'I do not know how I come to miss those two men. When we overtook them we had a clear shot at them and I fired three or four shots at the big negro but missed him every time. I am sorry I missed for I might have been able to save Downey's life.

"They did not get me on the first shot, but they would have had me sure if it had not been for the memorandum book in my left inside coat pocket. The bullet struck this book right over my heart and bruised but did not penetrate the skin. The ball was found in my drawers, where it had fallen."

The physicians have forbidden Downey's talking. He is able to take nourishment and is extremely conscious, but is suffering extreme pain. Mrs. Downey has been watching at his bedside constantly. As might be expected, she is rather disappointed that the crowd which went after the two men failed to secure them.

Judge Mason intends to call a special meeting of the Marion county bar to consider the advisability of calling a special grand jury to consider the indictment of the two negroes. He announces, however, that the case will not be tried until public feeling subsides and the men can obtain a fair and impartial trial.

Both Lilly and Downey are married, and have been in the service of the Baltimore & Ohio several years. Lilly is a detective and has been instrumental in running down many criminals, but was never fired upon before. Downey is night yardmaster at Fairmont.

The colored assailants, Albert Thorn and George Campbell, who are now at Wheeling, are said to be habitual criminals. Since their arrest detectives of the Pennsylvania system have asked for descriptions of the two men, believing they are the parties who killed one of their brakemen near Pittsburg not long ago. If Downey does not die the two men may be turned over to the Pennsylvania authorities for trial for murder.
albert-thomas-fairmont-1900-08-11.A17:
DOWNEY. IMPROVING.
The Fairmont Man is Now in Much Better Condition.
Henry Downey, the Fairmont B. & O. man who was shot and frightfully wounded by negro tramps in the Fairmont yards several weeks ago, is improving much better now than he did for the first three weeks after the shooting says the Wheeling News. He is at the city hospital and this morning it was stated that he had recovered much of his strength. While he will be unable to return to Fairmont for some days, he is completely out of danger. The men who shot Downey and a companion are still in the county jail here awaiting trial at Fairmont.

avery-mills-forest-city-1900-08-28.A1:
LYNCHED HIM FOR MURDER. FATAL QUARREL AS TO A TENANT'S RIGHTS THE CAUSE OF IT. Avery Mills, a Negro, of Forest City, N. C., Shoots M. H. Flack, His Landlord, for Trespass—Flack Calls for Mills's Blood—Mob Attends to It on the Way to Jail.
Mob Attends to It on the Way to Jail.

CHARLOTTE, N. C., Aug. 28.—A negro named Avery Mills was taken from the peace officers near Forest City, N. C., at noon to-day and riddled with bullets by a mob, which sought to avenge the death of Mills H. Flack, a former member of the Legislature and a well-known citizen of Rutherford county, who was shot and killed by Mills about 9 o'clock this morning. Three days ago Flack went to his plantation, which is rented to Mills, or who, by some agreement, is making a crop this year, to get some fruit, whereupon Mills's wife ordered him off. He refused to go and she went to the house and secured a pistol and went back the second time and ordered him to leave. He left rather than have a difficulty.

This morning at 9 o'clock Flack, his son Otho, and another boy went to the plantation in a wagon to pull fodder. Mills's house is about one hundred yards from the road. He appeared and halted Mr. Flack and began to renew the talk about the fruit, when Mills's wife brought him his pistol. He took it and shot Flack just under the heart. Flack, having a shotgun, drew and fired, the shot taking effect in the negro's shoulder. Flack then took the gun and pounded the negro over the head with it until it was broken.

The negro attempted to shoot Flack's son, but he hit the negro on the head with a stone and took his pistol away from him and shot him in the hip. The negro was not hurt badly. Flack died in less than an hour.

The news soon spread and the Forest City people were gathered at the scene. The negro and his wife were arrested. Flack said to his friends before he died that he could not live long, that the negro had killed him and that he wanted him hanged and wanted his friends to see it done. He was then taken home and the negro and his wife brought before a Justice, who at once committed them to jail. They were placed in the custody of Town Marshal Hamrick and Constable Hardin. A crowd overtook them two and one-half miles from Forest City. Sheriff Martin, leading another crowd, was on the way, but stopped down the road a few hundred yards to keep the people back. Meantime the first crowd had held up the wagon, and were waiting for a second squad. The Town Marshal, who was driving, attempted to push on, but the small crowd held him and told him not to move. The crowd was appealed to to let the negro alone and let him go to jail and take the full course of law, and at the time it seemed as if they would submit, but some one would then make a remark about the killing and stir the crowd again.

Finally the Marshal in charge of the wagon drew his revolver and started his horses, but just then a fresh body of horsemen arrived and yelled to the mob to take hold of the negro. The officers were pushed aside and the negro dragged from the wagon. After allowing him to sit down for five minutes the prisoner was marched off about a hundred yards from the road. A volley was fired at him, bringing instant death.
avery-mills-forest-city-1900-08-28.A4:
NEGRO LYNCHED.
Mob Also After a Black Woman Who Aided the Colored Man.
CHARLOTTE, N. C., Aug. 28.—A negro was lynched at Forest City, N. C., to-day, for the murder of a white man named Flack. Threats were also made to lynch a negro woman who had taken the gun to the murderer, and a mob went in search of her.
avery-mills-forest-city-1900-08-28.A5:
TENANT KILLS LANDLORD
Flack Sought to Frighten the Negro Who Shot Him.
THE NEGRO WAS ARRESTED AT ONCE
On the Way to the Jail a Mob Appeared,
Took the Negro from the Officers
and Filled Him with
Buckshot.
(Special to News and Observer.)

Charlotte, N. C., August 28.—Mills Flack, ex-member of the State Legislature, was shot to death at 9 o'clock this morning near Rutherfordton, by Avery Mills, a young negro, about 21 years of age. Flack had gone to Mills' house to get some fruit, Mills being his tenant. Mills refused to allow the fruit to be taken. Flack, who had a shot gun in his hand, fired it off in order, it is thought, to frighten the negro. Mills then had his wife to bring him a pistol, and opened on Flack, shooting him dead.

It is stated that Flack had no idea the negro intended killing him.

Mills was then arrested, and was being taken to jail when a mob of about 100 men appeared, took the negro from the officers, and emptied several loads of buckshot into his body. Mills' wife has been arrested as an accessory to the crime.

Parties from Rutherfordton state that the mob went about its work in the most orderly manner. There seemed to be very little excitement. Mills' wife says she does not know a single man who was in the mob, although no disguises were used.

After killing Mills the mob quietly dispersed and went to their homes.
avery-mills-forest-city-1900-08-28.A12:
LYNCHING OF A NEGRO.
Death of a Prominent North Carolinian Soon Avenged.
Charlotte, N. C. Aug. 28 — A brutal
Death of a Prominent North Carolinian Soon Avenged.

Charlotte, N. C., Aug. 28. — A brutal murder was followed by a lynching at Forest City, a short distance from Charlotte, this afternoon. The murdered man was Mills H. Flack, a prominent citizen of Rutherford county and a member of the State Legislature. The man who was lynched for the crime was Avery Mills, a well-known negro of that section.

Flack had been missing peaches from his orchard. Circumstances seemed to point to Mills as the thief. Flack met Mills this afternoon and accused him. Mills drew a pistol and shot Flack, the bullet entering the body near the heart, causing death almost instantly. Flack's body was soon found at a point near his house, and Mills was captured an hour afterward.

An armed mob took the negro from the officers, swung him to a tree and then riddled his body with bullets. Mills is said to have been a desperate character, and his victim was one of the most popular men in the State.

Negro Killed His Employer and Was Shot to Pieces.

Flack, ex-state representative, was shot and instantly killed at his plantation at 9 o'clock this morning, near Forest City, seven miles from here, by his negro renter, Avery Mills. Mills was quickly arrested and almost as quickly taken from the officers while on the way to jail, carried 100 yards from the main road and riddled with bullets by a mob of about twelve, though there were fifty or more followers.

Flack shot the negro with his shotgun and broke it into pieces over his head. Young Flack took the pistol and shot the negro in the hip but not seriously injuring him. SLAYER OF MR. FLACK VICTIM OF MOB'S VENGEANCE.
Rutherfordton, N. C., Aug. 30.—Mr. Mills H. Flack was shot and killed on his plantation, near Forest City, this morning at 9 o'clock by Avery Mills, a negro, and later Mills and the officers in charge of him were overtaken by a crowd on the way to Rutherfordton jail and the negro carried to the woods and riddled with bullets.

It seems that three days ago Mr. Flack went to his plantation, which is rented to Mills, or who is, by some agreement, making a crop this year, to get some fruit, whereupon Mills' wife ordered him off. He refused to go and she went to the house and secured a pistol and went back the second time and ordered him to leave. He left rather than have a difficulty. This morning at 9 o'clock Mr. Flack, his son, Otho, and another boy went to the plantation in a wagon to pull fodder. Mills' house is about 100 yards from the road. He appeared and halted Mr. Flack and began to renew the talk about the fruit, when Mills' wife brought him his pistol. He took it and deliberately shot Mr. Flack just under the heart. Mr. Flack, having a shotgun, drew it and fired, the shot taking effect in the negro's shoulder, and then took the gun and pounded the negro over the head with it until it was broken. The negro attempted to shoot Mr. Flack's son, but he hit the negro in the head with a rock and took his pistol away from him and shot him in the hip. The negro was not hurt badly.

Mr. Flack died in less than an hour. The news soon spread and the Forest City people were gathered at the scene. The negro and his wife were arrested. Mr. Flack said to his frinds before he died that he could not live long; that the negro had killed him, and that he wanted him hanged and wanted his friends to see it done. He was then taken home and the negro and wife brought before Justice J. C. Green, who at once committed them to jail. They were placed in the custody of Town Marshal Hamrick and Constable Hardin.
After learning of the affair, the reporter started to Forest City to learn the particulars, and reaching the Seaboard Air Line depot, at Forest City, met the officers and prisoner coming to jail. Not stopping, but going on toward the city, I saw crowds on horseback and in vehicles armed and coming at full speed. I returned and overtook the officers and prisoners and informed them that an eager-looking crowd of men were pursuing them. They moved on as rapidly as possible, but the crowd overtook them just two and one-half miles from Forest City, at the old Eaves place, on the right of the Seaboard Air Line road. Sheriff Martin, leading another crowd, was on way, and stopped down the road a few hundred yards to keep them back. In the meantime the first crowd had held up the wagon, and were waiting for a second squad. The town marshal, who was driving, attempted to push on, but the small crowd held the horse and told him not to move.

negro alone, and let him go to jail and take the full course of law, and at the time it did seem that they would submit, but some one would then make a remark about the killing and stir the crowd again.

Town Marshal J. D. Justice, of Rutherfordton, made the crowd a most sensible talk: as also did Mr. O. C. Erwin and Constable Hardin. They tried to persuade them, one at a time. Mr. Justice told Marshal Hamrick to drive on. He got in his wagon, took out his revolver and told the crowd that he was a marshal and had the prisoner in charge and was going to take him to jail. He started to drive a second time, but was stopped, and one of the crowd pulled the negro out of the back end of the wagon. He was left sitting there a few minutes, and then, when more men arrived, one man called out: "Grab him up!" and so they did in the midst of all the pleading that could be done, and took him down the road.

When the mob had gotten the negro out of the wagon Sheriff Martin was coming close behind with the officers, and some one yelled, "There comes the sheriff!" Immediately the negro was thrown against the bank of the road and the small mob ahead began firing, and he was dead in less than a minute. He groaned once and kicked once.

The firing had hardly ceased before the crowd was quickly making its way through the woods. The sheriff was very much surprised and worried over the affair. The crowd that did the shooting did not number over a dozen. About 20 shots took effect.

Two Negroes Shot.
MONTGOMERY, Ala., Aug. 23.—Two negroes, badly shot, were brought to this city from Flomaton for medical treatment. Just how the wounds were inflicted is not known. One report is that several negro tramps were discovered in an empty box car and when ordered out resisted and a general fight followed, several of them being wounded. Another report is that there was a clash between the whites and blacks at Flomaton and that the two railroad negroes were shot.

NEWPORT NEWS.
STEEL PLANT ASSURED - NEGRO KILLED-ELKS BASEBALL GAME.
Newport News, Va., Aug. 6.—Mr. C. P. Huntington's hobby—the establishment of a steel plant in this city for the manufacture of the material used in the construction of ships at the shipyard—bids fair to soon assume definite proportions. Mr. Huntington, who is in the city on one of his periodical trips of inspection, said yesterday that he had finally decided to build the plant, and while it would not be the largest establishment of the kind in the country, it would cost in the neighborhood of $1,000,000 and would give employment to a large force of men. He refused to say when work on the new plant would be started, but positively asserted that the plant had been decided upon and that it would soon assume definite shape. He said that further investigation of the armor-plate situation had convinced him that it was impracticable for builders of warships to manufacture their own armor-plate, and that if a factory for this product is established here it would not be in connection with his enterprises. The steel plant is to be located on the lots directly in front of the general offices of the ship-building plant. These lots have been excavated, the dirt being used to fill in the approaches to the Lafayette avenue bridge. The plant will be built on both sides of the ship-yard switch, so that material may be readily handled on incoming and outgoing trains.

ELKS TO PLAY ELKS.

A special from Richmond says: "The challenge of the Newport News Elks to the Richmond Elks for a game of ball has been enthusiastically accepted by the B. P. O. E. of Richmond, and Jake Wells is organizing a team from the Elks here to send to Newport News. The date has not been fixed, but when they come Newport News will have a jolly crowd on her hands.

The Richmond Elks feel particularly kindly to the Newport News Elks because of the earnest and staunch support they gave them in their fight at Atlantic City for the national convention. The conduct of the Newport News Elks was in strong contrast to the action of members of the order from other Virginia cities, and in recognition of their cordial support then.
A NEGRO KILLED.

A negro man known as "Coffee," and whose rightful name cannot be learned. was killed here last night by Policeman R. B. Payne. He and three other negroes were playing craps when surprised by a sergeant and two officers, one of whom was Payne.

On the way to the station-house "Coffee" made a break for liberty. Payne started in pursuit and when the fugitive paid no heed to his orders to halt, fired three_shots after him, apparently without effect. Payne then then rejoined the main party and went to the station-house with them.

An hour later the sergeant stumbled over "Coffee's" body in a dark corner, and had it it removed to the dark station. An inquest held held yesterday to the station. An inquest
verdict in accordance with these facts. Policeman Payne will be given a preliminary hearing to-morrow. He is out on bail.

NEWPORT NEWS.
At the shipyards of H. M. Bean the largest schooner in the world will be launched on August 14. She is a sixmaster. Captain John G. Crowley is the managing owner, and Arthur Crowley is her captain."

The new vessel is 2,750 tons net register, 300 feet long on her oak keel, 335 feet long over all, 46 feet beam and 26 feet deep. She will ply between Newport News and Philadelphia, carrying 5,500 tons of coal in her hold.

Her six masts are of Oregon pine, each 116 feet long, with 58-foot topmasts. The lower masts are 26 inches in diameter in the partners, except the foremast, which is 30 inches. The foretopmast is 20 inches in the cap, and the others 17 inches. The bowsprit is 35 feet long, and the jibboom 75 feet. She has a forward house 26 feet long, midship house 16 feet and an afterhouse 35 feet, besides a large wheelhouse.

The vessel is fitted with a double set of pumps, with engines and steam winches fore and aft.

A new feature is the keelson, extending to the lower deck beams, making a solid backbone 13½ feet high.

CANNOT BRING SUIT.

Under a ruling of the Railroad Commissioner, Mr. H. S. Baker, the penitentiary guard who was made to get off a Chesapeake and Ohio train last week because he would not take into the colored coach a negro prisoner he was bringing to the prison, cannot recover damages from the company, and suit will not be instituted. The Railroad Commissioner is required by law to contract with the various transportation companies to cary prisoners to and from from the prison. The contracts with all roads provide expressly that convicts and lunatics may be restricted to such passenger coaches as the conductor in charge of the train may designate.

POLICEMAN PAYNE GOES FREE.
Newport News Officer Who Killed Escaping Crap Player Exonerated.
Newport News, Va., Aug. 9.—In the police court to-day Judge Brown took up the case of Officer R. B. Payne, charged with the murder of the negro crap player, John Williams, alias "Coffee," last Saturday night. After hearing the testimony, which was the same adduced at the coroner's inquest, and the officer's statement, Judge Brown dismissed the charge and Payne resumed his place on the police force.

Judge Brown held that an officer is justified in shooting an escaping prisoner, no matter upon what specific charge the fugitive may have been arrested.

william-ford-martinsburg-1900-08-20.A1:
A LIVELY TIME.
Officer Dutrow Has a Long Chase. Fires Down Main Street.
Great excitement was caused on the main thoroughfare of the city a few minutes past seven o'clock p.m. Monday by the somewhat unusual sight of a negro running down Main street followed by a blue-coat and a bullet, the latter, of course, traveling a little faster than the wearer of the blue, but not hiting its mark. The chase, the shooting and the subsequent arrest of the pursued by the pursurer, caused universal excitement and a general outbreak of lawlessness was looked for at any minute. The colored population was enraged at the act of the officer in firing at his intended prisoner and the white people who congregated on the street were indignant by the stubborn resistance offered to the officer by the prisoner and the remarks of his colored friends, which were heard here and there in the crowd. It would have taken the slightest provocation to fan the sparks of anger into flames of conflict, resulting in a general race riot. Happily the danger period was passed, however, and about an hour afterwards affairs assumed a normal shape again.

The originator of the trouble was William Ford, a transfer-wagon driver for whom Policeman Dutrow has had a warrant since Friday. Ford and another baseball player, Arthur Fisher, got into an altercation over a baseball game at Randolph Ramer's restaurant Friday night. Officer Dutrow got onto the scrap and had warrants issued for the scrappers. He was unable to find either of them until last evening, however. In walking down East Martin street he saw Ford and walked toward him. Ford started for the opposite side of the street. Officer Dutrow overtook him and imparted to him the unwelcome information that he had a warrant for his arrest. Ford would not listen to the proposition to accompany the officer until the warrant was read to him. The officer proceeded to do so and while handling the papers he looked up to see that his bird had flown.

The fleeing prisoner turned southward at Queen with Dutrow in pursuit. Chief of Police Freeze and his dog also took a hand in the chase. When the fleeing man was about the middle of the square Officer Dutrow, who was a good distance behind him, pulled his gun and fired. The bullet flew wild of its mark. Bystanders say they heard it strike the People's Bank building, haying traveled almost the entire length of the square without striking anything or any one.

The fleet-footed runner seemed to be impelled onward all the swifter by the noise of the bullet singing a merry tune past him. He turned eastward at the corner of Queen and Burke, ran to Water street and then turned southward again. In going down the Burke street hill the officer came across a buggy, which he got into and resumed the chase with greater celerity. By this time a crowd had collected and, yelling and whooping, joined in the chase. It is said that the fleeing man had to dodge a number of stones thrown at him on Water street by people endeavoring to stop him.

The space between the purser and pursued was rapidly made shorter after the officer got into the buggy and on East John street in the yard of Jacob Custer he finally came up to his man. He had just climbed over the fence, when Officer Dutrow arrived and leveled his gun at his prisoner. The latter was overawed this time by seeing the muzzle of the gun staring him in his face, with the officer's hand upon the trigger and the nippers were soon upon his wrist.

The march back to the lock-up, which also proved to be very interesting, was then resumed, the two followed by a large crowd of colored and white men and boys. Everything passed off alright until Queen street was reached, when, while walking along the street, the prisoner gave the officer a shove and threw him into the street he had pulled.
Another provoking incident occurred at the corner of Queen and Martin streets earlier in the evening. A young man from the country, D. H. Baker, was walking past the corner, when Frank Sampson, colored, better known as "Chub," without any provocation or warning, hauled away and struck him, knocking him to the pavement. The man got up and meekly walked away, probably afraid to offer fight amid such a crowd of colored people as was on the corner.

Officer McBee arrived a few minutes later and gave chase to Sampson, chasing him as far as Maple avenue and then turning back. He had a warrant sworn out for him and when he went off duty turned it over to Officer Durrow, who arrested him about nine o'clock in the evening.
